idiom_name: Iterator[A] from Iterator.iterate / Iterator.unfold / custom hasNext-next
implementation_notes: Scala provides lazy production instead of a generator statement: Iterator[A] is a single-pass pull sequence (hasNext/next) with the full collection API, built from Iterator.iterate(start)(f) for state-driven series, Iterator.unfold(seed)(step) (2.13) for seed-plus-step generation, Iterator.continually(value) for constants, or a hand-written hasNext/next pair. Nothing runs until a terminal operation forces elements, and View gives the same laziness over an existing collection; choose LazyList (variant) when the sequence must be replayable.
code_sketch:
val fib: Iterator[BigInt] =          // lazy, single pass
  Iterator.iterate((BigInt(0), BigInt(1))) { case (a, b) => (b, a + b) }.map(_._1)

fib.take(10).foreach(println)        // only ten steps are computed
pitfalls: Iterator extends IterableOnce: any traversal consumes it, so a second call on the same Iterator returns nothing (or throws), and even toString used while debugging can eat the first element.

Operations that need the whole sequence (groupBy, sortWith, size on a large source) buffer internally, and reusing one iterator in two places of a single expression is a common silent-empty bug - assign a fresh iterator per pass.

variants.name: LazyList (memoized lazy sequence)
variants.idiom_name: LazyList from LazyList.unfold / LazyList.iterate / #:: lazy cons
variants.implementation_notes: LazyList keeps already-forced elements, so it can be traversed again and shared between consumers at the cost of retaining the computed prefix; build it with LazyList.unfold(seed)(step), LazyList.iterate(start)(f) or a #:: cons chain, and take(n)/force compute only what is asked. Choose it over Iterator when replayability or multiple consumers matter and the forced prefix is small enough to memoize; prefer Iterator when the sequence is large, one-shot or effectful.
variants.code_sketch:
val fib: LazyList[BigInt] =          // memoized lazy sequence
  LazyList.unfold((BigInt(0), BigInt(1))) { case (a, b) => Some((a, (b, a + b))) }

val first10 = fib.take(10).force     // forces only ten elements
fib(100)                             // memoized prefix is reused
pitfalls: Memoization retains the forced prefix: keeping a reference to the head of a long or infinite LazyList leaks memory unless intermediate nodes are dropped, and effectful generation is replayed (or not) in ways callers rarely expect.

LazyList replaced Stream (deprecated since 2.13) because Stream evaluated tails eagerly in surprising places; migrated code that depended on Stream's evaluation points can force more elements than intended.
